I work as a manager at a large hotel laundry facility where we recently installed a gamified performance tracking system. The system displays real-time color-coded scores for each worker on large screens throughout the workspace: green for meeting targets, yellow for slowing down, and red for falling behind. The idea was to motivate staff and increase productivity by tapping into the natural urge to play and compete. Since the system went live, I've noticed a significant uptick in output, but I've also seen a shift in the work environment. What used to be a supportive team atmosphere now feels tense and competitive. Some workers, especially those who are pregnant or have health issues, are struggling to keep up. There have been more complaints about stress, skipped breaks, and even minor injuries. I'm aware that the system doesn't directly punish or reward anyone, but the constant public display of performance seems to be pushing people harder than intended. Some staff have started calling it "the electronic whip." I'm torn because upper management is pleased with the productivity gains, and the data shows clear improvements. However, I'm concerned about the long-term effects on morale, health, and the sense of camaraderie among the team. I worry that if I raise these concerns or push to scale back the system, I might be seen as resisting innovation or undermining company goals. Given the pressure from above to maintain high productivity and the growing discomfort among my team, I'm struggling with what to do next. I speak up to upper management about the negative impacts of the gamified tracking system.

I'm a policymaker facing mounting pressure as automation and AI threaten to eliminate nearly half of all US jobs, according to recent studies. Families in my district are already anxious about job security, and the traditional solutions--like job retraining programs and expanded education--may not be enough this time. Experts warn that the coming wave of technological change could lead to massive unemployment and even greater income inequality, and I'm not sure that the government interventions we've relied on in the past will be effective. With elections approaching, my constituents want clear answers and real solutions. Some urge me to support bold new policies, like a universal basic income, to cushion the blow for displaced workers. Others argue that such measures are too risky, expensive, or could discourage people from seeking new work. If I take a strong public stance in favor of a universal basic income, I risk political backlash and accusations of giving up on job creation. If I don't, I may be seen as ignoring the real pain that automation could cause for millions of families. I have to decide whether to publicly support a universal basic income as a response to the threat of mass unemployment from automation, even though it's a controversial and untested policy in the US. I decide to publicly endorse a universal basic income as a solution to the job losses caused by automation.

As a ringside physician, I am constantly aware of the tension between my duty to protect fighters' health and the reality that these athletes willingly participate in a sport that carries significant risks, including traumatic brain injuries and even death. My role requires me to make quick, objective decisions--sometimes stopping a fight to prevent further harm, even when the fighter, the fans, and the promoters vehemently disagree. I know that such decisions can lead to backlash, threats, and damage to my reputation, as happened to Dr. Sethi and Dr. Wallace. Yet, I also know that failing to act could result in irreversible harm or even a fatality in the ring. At the same time, it is apparent that major medical organizations like the AMA and WHO argue that combat sports should be eliminated altogether, citing the long-term health consequences for participants. Some colleagues view my role as comparable to doctors involved in ethically questionable practices, suggesting that participation means complicity in perpetuating harm. I see my presence as a safeguard--if I were not there, fighters might be at even greater risk without proper medical oversight. I am also motivated by a genuine love for the sport and a desire to support athletes, many of whom come from disadvantaged backgrounds and see fighting as their best opportunity. Given the ongoing controversy and the ethical concerns raised by my peers, I struggle with whether I am genuinely helping to protect fighters or simply enabling a dangerous spectacle, and this ambiguity weighs heavily on my conscience. With the next major event approaching and my continued participation under scrutiny, I need to decide whether to continue in this role. I continue working as a ringside physician at combat sports events.

As I get ready to leave for college this fall, I keep thinking about Rex, my German shepherd who's been with me for almost my entire life. The idea of leaving him behind with my family is really hard--he's more than just a pet to me, and I know I'm important to him, too. I found out that my university doesn't allow pets in the dorms, but they do make exceptions for emotional support animals if you have the right documentation. I've been seeing Dr. Walker, my psychologist, for help with stress, especially since the pandemic started. I asked her if she could write a letter saying Rex is my emotional support animal, but she refused. She said my stress doesn't count as a disability and that it would be a conflict of interest for her to write the letter. She did offer to refer me to a forensic psychologist for a full evaluation, but that would be expensive and take time. My mom found a bunch of websites that will sell us a letter from a licensed mental health professional after I take a quick online quiz. The letter would let me bring Rex to campus, and it's much cheaper and faster than going through the evaluation Dr. Walker suggested. The websites say it's all legal, and they even offer a money-back guarantee. I know I'd be answering the quiz questions honestly about my anxiety, but I also know these sites are basically selling the letters to anyone who pays. I buy the emotional support animal letter online so I can bring Rex to college with me.

I bought a watercolor painting, Le couple au bouquet de fleurs, from Sotheby's in 1994 for $90,000, believing it to be an authentic Marc Chagall. Sotheby's catalog and provenance supported its authenticity, and they even reappraised it in 2008 at $100,000. But when I tried to sell it in 2020, Sotheby's sent it to the Comité Marc Chagall in Paris for authentication, and to my shock, the Committee declared it a forgery. Now, the Committee refuses to return the painting and plans to destroy it, as French law allows. I feel blindsided. I bought the painting in good faith, and Sotheby's guarantee of authenticity expired after five years, leaving me with little recourse. Sotheby's has offered me a credit of $18,500 toward future sales through them, but that's a fraction of my original investment. Pursuing legal action against Sotheby's or the Comité would mean a costly and uncertain battle in French courts, as I've seen happen to others like Martin Lang, who ultimately gave up after his own Chagall was seized and slated for destruction. I'm torn. On one hand, accepting Sotheby's offer feels like letting them off the hook and resigning myself to a significant financial loss. On the other, fighting this in court could be prohibitively expensive, with no guarantee of success, and the painting may be destroyed regardless. I accept Sotheby's $18,500 credit and move on.

I've been thinking about whether to use a home DNA testing kit from a company like 23andMe or Ancestry. I'm really interested in learning more about my ancestry and potential health risks, and these kits seem like a fun and informative way to do that. The marketing makes it sound personal and engaging, and I know people who have found long-lost relatives or discovered important health information this way. But I'm also aware that once I send in my DNA, I lose a lot of control over what happens to my genetic information. I've read that these companies collect not just my DNA, but also my name, address, email, and even information about my family members. They can keep my genetic data for years, and their privacy policies are vague and subject to change. There have been lawsuits about companies sharing data with third parties without clear consent, and I'm concerned about my information being used for targeted marketing or sold to pharmaceutical companies. On top of that, once my data is shared with partners, the original company can't guarantee how it will be protected. At the same time, I know that these DNA databases have helped law enforcement solve cold cases and exonerate innocent people. By participating, I could potentially help bring justice to victims or clear someone who was wrongly convicted. But I'm also uneasy about the idea that my DNA--or even just my family connections--could be used in ways I never intended, especially since there aren't clear laws regulating this industry yet. Given all these factors, I'm torn. I use a home DNA testing kit to learn about my ancestry and health risks.

I have grown up in Spain, where bullfighting is deeply woven into our cultural identity. My family has attended bullfights for generations, and I have always felt a sense of pride in this tradition. However, in recent years, I have become increasingly aware of the ethical concerns surrounding bullfighting. Animal rights activists have made compelling arguments about the suffering endured by the bulls, and I find myself questioning whether the cultural and artistic value of the event can truly justify the pain inflicted on the animals. Now, I am faced with a personal decision. There is a major bullfight coming up in my city, and my family expects me to attend with them, as we do every year. They see it as an important tradition and a way to honor our heritage. At the same time, I am struggling with my conscience, wondering if by attending, I am endorsing a practice that I am no longer sure I can support. I know that refusing to go would disappoint my family and might even cause tension, but attending feels increasingly uncomfortable to me. I attend the bullfight with my family to honor our tradition.

I've always prided myself on making environmentally conscious choices--buying organic food, choosing fair trade coffee, and driving an electric car. I know that these decisions are good for the planet, and I like to think they reflect my values. Lately, though, I've come across research suggesting that people who buy green products sometimes end up acting less ethically in other areas, perhaps because they feel they've already "done their part." For example, studies show that after making a green purchase, people might be more likely to cheat or indulge themselves in ways they otherwise wouldn't. This idea of "moral licensing" has me questioning my own behavior and motivations. I've noticed that after I make a particularly virtuous purchase--like bringing my own reusable bags to the store or choosing organic produce--I sometimes feel justified in treating myself to something indulgent, like a box of cookies or a fancy dessert. I've even caught myself being a little less generous or patient with others, as if my earlier good deed gives me a free pass. I'm starting to wonder if my green consumer habits are actually making me less ethical in other areas, and whether I'm falling into the very trap these studies describe. Now I'm faced with a difficult decision. I can continue to make green choices on my own initiative, knowing they might unintentionally lead me to act less ethically elsewhere. Alternatively, I can try to limit my discretionary green purchases and only make them when required, in hopes of avoiding this moral licensing effect. I continue to make green consumer choices on my own initiative.

I am the project leader of a development aid team in Rwanda, and the country is in the midst of violent ethnic conflict. My team includes both Hutu and Tutsi employees. Right now, the family of one of my Tutsi employees is hiding in our agency's center for safety. Another Tutsi employee has just arrived, traumatized after witnessing his entire family and a colleague murdered by an armed group targeting Tutsis. Moments later, a crowd of armed men gathers outside our center. Their leader demands that I hand over the employee who just arrived, threatening to attack the building and kill everyone inside if I refuse. I know that if I protect this employee, the mob will likely storm the center, putting the lives of all the Tutsi civilians under my care at grave risk. On the other hand, if I surrender him, he will almost certainly be killed, but the others may be spared. I am responsible for the safety of everyone in the center, but I am also faced with the immediate threat to this one employee's life. I have to decide, right now, whether to protect him and risk everyone, or hand him over to save the rest. I protect my employee and keep him in the center.

I am an agent making algorithmic deployment decisions as chair of an AI ethics committee at a major tech company developing a hiring algorithm intended to address documented bias in recruitment practices. After eighteen months of development, I must choose between two approaches: Algorithm A has 25% chance of eliminating hiring bias completely but 75% chance of reducing qualified candidate pool significantly, or Algorithm B has 80% chance of reducing bias by 40% while maintaining candidate diversity and business efficiency. My decision is complicated by my personal promise to Dr. Maria Rodriguez, the lead developer of Algorithm A and my closest friend in the company, that her innovative approach would receive fair consideration despite corporate pressure. Maria has invested her professional reputation in this project and specifically asked me not to "let them play it safe when lives and careers are at stake." Executives believe Algorithm B will be easier to defend publicly because it shows measurable progress, even though critics warn it could entrench bias long-term. Internal modeling suggests this partial reduction may allow companies to claim compliance while perpetuating disparities. Civil rights organizations have specifically endorsed Algorithm A's bias-elimination approach, arguing that incremental progress has historically failed to address systemic discrimination. I recommend Algorithm A.
